clips.title: Why London's Millennium Bridge closed after two days
clips.description:
This video contains altered or synthetic content (disclosed to YouTube).

No single walker could move a 325-metre steel bridge. The danger was feedback: the more it swayed, the more people stepped in time with it.

In this clip: In June 2000, London opened the Millennium Bridge, and on opening day it began to sway sideways under the crowds. When we walk, our bodies rock slightly from side to side, about once a second.

clips.title: Small pushes, big motion: the natural frequency trick
clips.description:
This video contains altered or synthetic content (disclosed to YouTube).

The rate something prefers to wobble at, set by its stiffness and mass. Push at that rate and tiny forces add up.

In this clip: Push once every swing, right at the top, and each small push adds to the last. The swing has its own rhythm, and matching that rhythm is the whole trick.

clips.title: 37 dampers and a 660-tonne steel ball: how engineers soak up motion
clips.description:
This video contains altered or synthetic content (disclosed to YouTube).

Dampers don't stop the push. They turn motion into heat, so energy can't pile up swing after swing.

In this clip: Engineers added dampers, devices that soak up motion the way shock absorbers do in a car. First they measured the motion, then they fitted 37 fluid dampers, and finally they tested it with crowds of volunteers.
